segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he told them a parable about the need for them to pray always and not lose heart,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected any person.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In that city there was also a widow, and she kept coming to him, saying, ‘Give me justice against my opponent.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For a time he was unwilling, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Even though I do not fear God or respect any person,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: yet because this widow keeps causing me trouble, I will give her justice, so that she will not finally wear me out by her coming.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the Lord said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Listen to what the unjust judge says.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Will not God, then, bring about justice for his chosen ones who cry out to him day and night? Will he delay over them?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I tell you, he will bring about justice for them quickly. Yet when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also told this parable to some who were confident in themselves that they were righteous and looked down on the rest:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The Pharisee stood and prayed these words to himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of people—grasping, unjust, adulterous—or even like this tax collector.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of everything I acquire.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but kept beating his chest and saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, the sinner.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, but those who humble themselves will be exalted.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: People were bringing even their babies to him so that he might touch them, but when the disciples saw this, they rebuked them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus called for them, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let the little children come to me, and do not stop them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A certain leader asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Good teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery. Do not murder. Do not steal. Do not give false testimony. Honor your father and mother.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “All these I have kept since my youth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus heard this, he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “One thing you still lack. Sell everything you have and distribute it to the poor, and you will have treasure in the heavens; then come, follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he heard this he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Looking at him, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Indeed, it is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who heard this said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Then who can be saved?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is impossible for people is possible for God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Peter said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, we have left what was ours and followed you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: who will not receive back many times as much in this present time, and in the age to come eternal life.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking the Twelve aside, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be accomplished.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, and he will be mocked and insulted and spat on,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and after flogging him they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they understood none of this; the saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was being said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was approaching Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road, begging.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Hearing a crowd going by, he asked what this meant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he cried out,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent, but he shouted all the more,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Son of David, have mercy on me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus stopped and ordered that he be brought to him. When he came near, Jesus asked him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What do you want me to do for you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, I want to see again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “See again! Your faith has saved you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately he could see again, and he began to follow him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

notes.note: The verb literally means to strike someone under the eye, a term from boxing; Paul uses it of disciplining his body in 1 Corinthians 9:27. Most translators take it figuratively here, as “wear me out.” Others think the judge fears, perhaps with grim humor, that the widow will actually come and hit him, or that she will blacken his reputation. The phrase rendered “finally” can also mean “completely” or “continually.”

notes.traditional: though he bear long with them (KJV); Will he delay long over them? (RSV, ESV)
notes.note: The Greek is literally “and he is patient over them,” and its connection to the rest of the sentence is disputed. It may be a second question expecting the answer no, as rendered here, or a concession: “even though he is patient with them,” meaning either the chosen ones or their oppressors. A very similar phrase in Sirach 35, in a passage about God hearing the widow’s plea, favors the sense of delay.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” “justify” and “vindicate” all render the same group of words. In this chapter the widow’s “justice,” the “unjust” judge, the “unjust” people of the Pharisee’s prayer, those sure they are “righteous,” and the tax collector who goes home “justified” (verse 14) all belong to this group or are closely related to it. Both parables turn on who is truly in the right before God.

notes.traditional: stood and prayed thus with himself (KJV); standing by himself, prayed thus (ESV, NRSV)
notes.note: The phrase “to himself” can be attached to “prayed” (he prayed silently, or about himself) or to “stood” (he stood by himself, apart from the others). The manuscripts also vary in word order here. With verbs of speaking the phrase normally means “to himself,” which is the reading followed; many modern versions prefer “stood by himself.”

This is not the ordinary word for showing mercy that the blind man uses in verse 38. It belongs to the word-group used for atonement, and in the Septuagint this form appears in prayers asking God to pardon sins; its only other New Testament occurrence is Hebrews 2:17. Spoken in the temple, where atoning sacrifices were offered, the plea asks God to be reconciled to him.

The Greek has the definite article, “the sinner.” Most English versions render “a sinner,” treating the article as generic. It may instead be pointed: the tax collector sees himself as the sinner in the room, while the Pharisee compares himself favorably with everyone else. Grammarians are divided, and either rendering is defensible.

Traditionally “ruler,” which suggests a king or prince to a modern reader. The word covers anyone holding a position of authority, such as a magistrate, a synagogue official or a member of a governing council, and Luke does not say which this man was. The familiar description “rich young ruler” combines details from three Gospels; Luke does not call him young.

The word translated “eternal” is related to the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, as verse 30 makes explicit. It describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.”

The Greek is plural here, a Semitic turn of phrase that reflects Hebrew and Aramaic, where the word for heaven is always plural. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it for God’s dwelling; in verse 13 the word is singular.

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural it regularly refers to the non-Jewish peoples and is then translated “Gentiles.” Here it points to the Roman authorities, who carried out the mocking, flogging and execution described.

“Son of David” was a title for the Messiah, the expected king from David’s line. The blind man’s cry is therefore a public acclamation of Jesus as that king, made as Jesus nears Jerusalem. Luke records no one else addressing Jesus this way.

notes.traditional: hath saved thee (KJV); has made you well (ESV); has healed you (NIV)
notes.note: The verb means both “heal” or “rescue” and “save,” and it is the same word used in verse 26, “who can be saved?” Many modern versions render “has made you well” or “has healed you” here. “Saved” is kept so that the link is visible; Luke may well intend both the restored sight and something more, since the man at once follows Jesus.

candidates.reason: The verb covers physical healing, rescue and salvation, and versions split between “save,” “heal” and “make well” in the recurring formula “your faith has saved you,” hiding the link between healing stories and salvation sayings.
Traditional “ruler” suggests a monarch; the word recurs across the Gospels, Acts and the letters for officials, council members and synagogue heads and needs one policy.
Translations vary between “elect” and “chosen,” and the word recurs in the Gospels, Paul, 1 Peter and Revelation with theological weight.
Whether the plural is rendered “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” or “siblings” needs one policy across the Gospels and letters.
Versions vary between “of Nazareth,” “the Nazarene” and “the Nazorean,” and the form differs from Ναζαρηνός, so a single decision on both is needed.
